q: How do I calculate emissions from a freight invoice or lorry receipt?
title: Emissions from a freight bill or LR
short: Take the actual weight carried and the distance travelled from the lorry receipt, freight bill or e-way bill, multiply them to get tonne-kilometres, then multiply by a well-to-wheel emission factor for that transport mode. Use actual weight, not charged weight, and record where each number came from.

sections.h: Where each input sits on Indian paperwork
ul: Weight: the lorry receipt (LR, bilty or consignment note) shows actual weight and often a separate charged weight. Use actual weight. Charged weight can be a minimum or a volumetric figure.

Distance: the LR shows from and to. The e-way bill for the same consignment records the approximate distance in km, which is the best printed source. If neither has it, use a road distance between the two pincodes and note the tool used.
Mode and vehicle: the LR or e-way bill gives the vehicle number and mode (road, rail, air, ship). Vehicle size helps choose a truck factor.
The freight invoice itself: SAC 9965 (goods transport) or 9968 (courier), the amount and GST. The amount alone is not activity data.

p: Emissions (kg CO2e) = weight (tonnes) x distance (km) x emission factor (kg CO2e per tonne-km).

ISO 14083 and the GLEC Framework ask for well-to-wheel factors, which include fuel production as well as burning it. Take the factor from the GLEC default tables, your carrier's own data, or a sourced national figure, and write the source and edition next to the result.

ul: Part load: if your goods shared the truck, weight x distance already allocates by mass. Do not use the full truck's fuel.
Full truckload with fuel data: if the carrier gives litres of diesel for your trip, fuel x factor is more accurate than tonne-km.
Multi-leg shipments: calculate each leg (truck to port, ship, truck) with its own mode and distance, then add.
Empty return trips: GLEC default factors already assume typical empty running. Do not add them again.

p: Freight you pay a transporter for is Scope 3: Category 4 for inbound goods and outbound goods where you pay for the transport, Category 9 where the buyer pays. Your own trucks burning your own diesel are Scope 1, calculated from fuel slips instead.

example.title: Worked example: one truck consignment
lines: LR actual weight: 12 t (charged weight 15 t, ignored)
Factor (illustrative): 0.10 kg CO2e per tonne-km, well-to-wheel
example.note: The 0.10 factor is illustrative only. Replace it with a sourced road freight factor for the vehicle class, from the GLEC Framework or your carrier.

senseible: Senseible reads freight invoices and lorry receipts and classifies transport lines (SAC 9965, 9967 or 9968) as Scope 3 Category 4. A line gets a figure only when the weight, distance and mode are printed and an approved factor exists for that mode; otherwise it shows Needs Data instead of guessing from the amount.
